utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, would you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, case number IT-01-47-T, the Prosecutor versus Enver Hadzihasanovic and Amir Kubura.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Registrar. May we have the appearances, please, the Prosecution first.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President. Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning Counsel. For the Prosecution, Daryl Mundis, Ekkehard Withopf, and Ruth Karper, the case manager.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Withopf. And I'm turning towards the Defence counsel, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. President. Good morning, Your Honours. For the Defence of General Hadzihasanovic, Edina Residovic, counsel; Stephane Bourgon, co-counsel; and Mirna Milanovic, legal assistant. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. And the other counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. For the Defence of Mr. Kubura, Rodney Dixon, Fahrudin Ibrisimovic, and Mr. Mulalic, the legal assistant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. The Chamber would like to welcome all those present in the courtroom, the representatives of the Prosecution and of the Defence and the accused, and all the other personnel in the courtroom, including those helping us out outside and who are technically helping us to hold these proceedings. The Chamber would like to express its condolences to Mr. Kubura, who had a death in the family, and that is why General Kubura was authorised to attend his mother's funeral and that is why -- but we see him back here today. So we should like to express our condolences to General Kubura. Today we're going to continue with the video-conference witnesses and their testimony. We have two witnesses lined up for today. Let us just check to see whether we are online and can we hear the first witness. Mr. Withopf, could you tell us who the first witness that you will be calling is, or Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good morning, Your Honours, counsel. The first witness this morning is Jozo Markovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. The Chamber takes note of this. And may we have the witness ushered in, please, by the registrar. And Madam Registrar, please would you do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, sir. Can you hear me? Can you hear what I'm saying translated into your own language?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wasn't able to hear the interpretation. Can you give us your first and last name, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Jozo Markovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And what is your date of birth?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The 1st of January, 1930.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What is your profession or what job do you do at present?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm a farmer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're a farmer. That's what I heard. Now, in 1993, what were you doing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I always did the same kind of work.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you. Have you already testified before a tribunal, in court, or is this the first time that you're testifying?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I came here before, but I have never testified.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're now going to take the solemn declaration, and you will be reading from the card that the lady next to you is going to show you. Would you please read out what it says on the card in your own language.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. You may be seated, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We can see you on the screen, and you should be able to see us on the screen in front of you. Before we commence - and you'll be answering questions put to you by the Prosecution - I would like to give you some information to allow you to understand fully how these proceedings work. You will first be answering questions put to you by the representative of the Office of the Prosecutor. Try and answer the questions to the best of your ability, in complete form and precise form. If you don't know the answer, please say so. After that set of questions, other people will be asking you questions as well; that is to say, the lawyers of the accused. They will be asking you questions as well. So please do your best to answer as fully as possible. The Judges that you see before you on your screen can also ask you questions if they wish to do so. As you have just taken the solemn declaration, that entails consequences - that is to say, it is incumbent upon you to tell the truth. Should you give false testimony or lie, you will be subjecting yourself to consequences for perjury. And if you commit this violation, then a prison sentence of up to seven years can be proclaimed. The witness -- should the witness answer and think that by answering the question he will incriminate himself, then he has the right to remain silent. However, if the Judges ask you to answer, then you will not be subject to any consequences. Generally speaking, that is how the proceedings will be conducted, with you as the witness and testifying in that capacity. So without further ado, I'm going to give the floor to the representative of the Prosecution, who's going to start off by asking you some questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Examined by Mr. Mundis:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Markovic, my name is Daryl Mundis. I'm one of the Prosecutors in this case. I'm going to ask you some questions now. And if you don't understand my question or if you can't hear the question, please say so and I'll repeat the question. Sir, in 1993, where were you living?

utterances.speaker: JOZO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: In the village of Susanj, Zenica municipality.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you please tell the Trial Chamber what occurred in Susanj in June 1993.

utterances.speaker: JOZO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: What happened was there was an attack on the 8th of June, during the morning, early in the morning. But I wasn't in the village at that time. I was absent, because the week before I went to the point where they were holding Muslims and somebody from Zenica, a man whom I knew, came and I went over there, and the 7th Muslim changed and they put me in prison, and I spent the night in prison. They beat me up, and the next Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. day at around 10.00 in the evening they released me. So then I went to Zenica. They didn't let me go home, so I went to my sister's place in Zenica. And I was in Zenica for five or six days. I don't know exactly how long. And then I returned home.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Markovic, you just mentioned that you spent the night in prison. Can you please tell the Trial Chamber where you spent the night.

utterances.speaker: JOZO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: I belonged to the local community of Pojske. And it was in the school in that local community. And they turned that local community into a prison, and that night that I spent there - I spent the night there - there were perhaps 100 of us. And they released all the others but they just kept me. There were women. There were children. Any of the Croats that happened to pass by that way, they were all put in the prison in Pojske.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Markovic, do you recall after this period when you were in Zenica the date that you returned to Susanj?

utterances.speaker: JOZO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I said a moment ago. I spent some six or seven days there. I don't know exactly. Nobody was allowed to go, and I wasn't either, until I was released and allowed to go home.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you please tell the Trial Chamber what you saw when you returned to the village of Susanj in mid-June 1993.

utterances.speaker: JOZO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, the village had already been looted. Not all of it, but most of it. There was a lot of looting, and things were being damaged. I saw a group of boys who might have been 15 or 16 years old, and they had some long sticks in their hands and were busy breaking windows on the houses where the windows were still intact and hadn't been shattered.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters note that there is a great deal of interference. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Other than these 15- or 16-year-old boys, did you see anyone else involved in looting in the village?

utterances.speaker: JOZO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did. The village was full of people looting. I saw the police helping them too, helping them take property out of houses.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Markovic, when you say "property," can you tell the Trial Chamber what type of property you're referring to.

utterances.speaker: JOZO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, household goods and appliances, washing machines, fridges, household appliances. That's what I can say, the regular type of stuff that you could take out.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Markovic, did you personally witness any of these household goods being removed from houses?

utterances.speaker: JOZO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you please tell the Trial Chamber what you personally witnessed, including the person or persons who was removing the property.

utterances.speaker: JOZO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, mostly they were people I didn't know; although, some of them I did, but I would prefer not to mention their names, because they're neighbours, so it's not a good thing. But I did see some neighbours I knew, although mostly people came from other villages and I didn't know them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Markovic, at the time you returned to your village, were you living or staying in your own house?

utterances.speaker: JOZO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. When I returned - I forgot to say that a moment ago - I found my house and my son's house full of people. So all those people who didn't escape to Vitez were made to go to my village. My brother said, "I'm not going to flee," and other people went too. And people went to Ovnak, and that is the border between the municipalities of Zenica and Travnik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Markovic, you told us about people breaking windows. Did you observe any other type of damage being done to houses or other buildings?

utterances.speaker: JOZO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. People were taking goods out. And if they couldn't take them out, they would demolish them. They would take out the spare parts from washing machines, for example. Or, for example, my car remained behind, but they took the motor, the engine. So they would destroy and break everything that was in the houses. They would take the taps, for example. The things they could, they took; the others, they destroyed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Markovic, to your knowledge, was any property removed from your house?

utterances.speaker: JOZO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Later on. But I fled from my house, because I came during the day on one occasion and they beat me up. And then another time they put masks on their faces, like socks over their heads, and that's when I flew from my house. But my wife and my brother's wife stayed on in the house. I was in Zenica myself, but I would go home during the day. And one evening they turned up - the army, the soldiers - and they bashed in the door, smashed the windows, and my wife was injured and her face was all bloody and she even had to have an operation later on. She was injured from the glass. Then they looted my whole house. It's a little funny, but a barrel full of brandy was taken away. I never had much, but they took my brandy and my radio, and I had a lot of food. They took all that away. And they left the house almost empty. They didn't take the furniture. They just took clothing and this radio and the food we had.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Markovic, do you recall approximately when this was, when the soldiers bashed in the door and smashed the windows?

utterances.speaker: JOZO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: It's difficult to say. They just smashed in the door. They didn't smash the windows on that occasion. That time they just bashed in the door and forced their way in. And my wife and my brother's wife looked at them, and they locked themselves up in a room, but they broke through and took the goods.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Markovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: The Prosecution has no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Mundis. I give the floor now to the Defence counsel for their cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Cross-examined by Ms. Residovic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Markovic. Can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: JOZO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: I can.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I am Edina Residovic, and I am representing General Enver Hadzihasanovic. I would like to ask you kindly to answer a few questions for me. You told my learned friend from the OTP that you were born and that you lived in the village of Susanj; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JOZO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The village of Susanj belongs to the municipality of Zenica and is situated north from the main road running from Zenica towards Travnik; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JOZO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your village was mostly inhabited by Croats; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JOZO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Not far from your village of Susanj there are other Croat villages, such as Ovnak, Novo Selo, Grahovcici, and Cukle; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JOZO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. But they don't belong to Zenica. They belong to Travnik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. They are very close to your village, but they belong to another municipality, the municipality of Travnik; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JOZO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that on the 8th of June a conflict broke out in your village as well. Is it true that before the 8th of June, 1993 there were no conflicts in your village and the surroundings between the army and the HVO? Is that right?

utterances.speaker: JOZO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: However, there were some problems nevertheless because you heard that in other parts, not far from your village, there had been clashes between the BH army and the Croatian Defence Council, so that the population of the village did feel fear; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JOZO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: That was closer to Travnik, I think.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You also knew that along the road going from Zenica towards Travnik there were checkpoints which did not allow freedom of movement, is that right, free passage?

utterances.speaker: JOZO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. For a while they did allow movement, but when this attack came on Susanj and the other villages, then no one was allowed to pass.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it true that the HVO had a checkpoint at Ovnak and that it checked everyone moving from Zenica towards Travnik at that checkpoint?

utterances.speaker: JOZO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: There was a checkpoint. Now, whether they searched people, I don't know. I wasn't interested, nor was I there. But there was a checkpoint, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your village, the able-bodied men belonged to the Frankopan HVO Brigade; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOZO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This brigade had its headquarters in Guca Gora and a company in Grahovcici; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JOZO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: I'm not sure about these things. I know about Grahovcici. There was some sort of a unit. But about Guca Gora, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your sons, Fabijan and Zoran, were members of the HVO; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JOZO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You personally were not a member of the HVO, but you were issued a Kalashnikov automatic rifle; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JOZO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The tension in the village was intensified after the Jure Francetic Brigade was disarmed in Zenica and after -- the area Ovnak-Grahovcici -- many people had come, both inhabitants and the members of the Jure Francetic Brigade from Zenica had come there; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JOZO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know whether there were soldiers. There were refugees who were expelled from there. About the other things, I don't know. I wasn't following these things.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After April, many people in your village became scared that there would be fighting in your village too, so that most of the villagers withdrew to Grahovcici where this HVO company was based; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JOZO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, some did flee. Whether people stayed behind, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: However, you and your immediate family remained in the village of Susanj; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JOZO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Just myself and my wife.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You know that the local authorities from Zenica, together with the European monitors and the priests from your parish in Zenica, talked to the people, the refugees, trying to persuade them to go back to Zenica where their safety would be guaranteed. Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: JOZO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know that. As far as the church is concerned, we belonged to Brajkovici.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your villagers from Susanj, your neighbours who had gone towards Brajkovici, or at least a part of them, at the end of April returned to the village again; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JOZO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know that they returned. I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the 8th of June, you said that early in the morning you heard shooting in the distance; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JOZO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No, I'm sorry. I'm sorry. I made a mistake. I'll rephrase that. On the 8th of June itself, you were not in the village of Susanj. You were in Zenica. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: JOZO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Though you wanted to go back, but in the days immediately following the 8th of June you were not allowed to do that because they told you that it was dangerous in view of the fighting, that it was dangerous for you to go to Susanj alone; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JOZO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you did return to Susanj several days after the fighting ceased, in your house you found your wife and some other villagers, quite a number of them; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JOZO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Just the women. There were a few older men. All the women had been shepherded into my house and my son's house, because I'm at the bottom of the village. My house is almost the first you reach going from Zenica. It is at the end of the village, but it belongs to Susanj.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it true, Mr. Markovic, that your wife and the other villagers who were in your house told you that the soldiers had put them up into your house and your son's house because it was removed and sheltered from the fighting going on in the village? Is that right?

utterances.speaker: JOZO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: There were few Croats left. They had all fled. When the fighting had stopped, they rounded them up from the houses and put them in these houses. My brother remained and some other men. They were all executed, those who stayed behind in the village. No one dared stay. I plucked up courage and returned.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You just heard that during those combat activities and after that several locals of your village had been killed. But you personally were not a witness of those killings, were you?

utterances.speaker: JOZO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: I wasn't a witness, but I was a witness of the bodies brought to the morgue by the civil defence, and I went there with my two nephews. We put 19 men into coffins in the morgue. That, I'm a witness of. I know. I heard from others.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Actually, you were just a witness of the identification of the bodies that were already in the morgue in Zenica; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JOZO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In answer to a question from my learned friend, you already said that when you returned your house was not damaged; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JOZO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. But it was looted. Soldiers forced their way in, broke down the door. They hit my wife with glass on the head. My wife and my brother's wife wouldn't let them in. These were soldiers. They were drunk. They were bullies. But they were soldiers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. But the event you are now describing occurred much later and not when you came back to Susanj after the conflict; is that right? This event happened after the other villagers had left your house and your son's house; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JOZO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You don't know the exact date when that happened, but this did not happen immediately after the combat activities; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JOZO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you returned several days after the battle, your wife told you that shells had fallen on the village, that there was a lot of fighting, and that two houses in the village had been destroyed and burnt by shelling; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JOZO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: The soldiers set fire to them, not the shells. Tomo Markovic's house is considered to have been burnt by shelling. The others were set on fire by soldiers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you came to your house, a delegation from Zenica came to visit you, and among them was the vice-president of the executive board of the municipal assembly, representatives of the civilian police, and a lawyer; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JOZO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't remember that there was a lawyer. Various people came to see me, but I can't name any of them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So delegations came to see whether you were safe and to suggest to the people to move to Zenica because they could not fully guarantee your safety from various gangs that were going around.

utterances.speaker: JOZO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Is that what you're saying, that we were advised to go to Zenica?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The villagers in your house were advised to go to Zenica. Because of various gangs roaming the village at night, they couldn't protect you. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: JOZO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: No. They told the police to take care of me. And they were forced to go to Zenica, and there was fear. And people were fleeing. When the dead people were buried, a bus took us from Zenica to the cemetery and we buried the dead. And they were forced into the bus and they were taken to Zenica and it was safer there. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But people wanted to go to Zenica, and they entered the buses one on top of another because they were afraid.

utterances.speaker: JOZO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: They were scared. They were fleeing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But the civilian authorities of Zenica municipality assigned a civilian police platoon to protect yourself and the village, but the area was vast and this police unit could not prevent the looting that was going on; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JOZO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: It couldn't. How could they prevent it when they took part in the looting? The police did. I saw myself. They masked their faces once. And I fled. And a policeman who was assigned to protect me, and my wife said to him, "Can't you see what they're doing?" And he said, "Don't be afraid. They won't hurt you." Karan Sajo, Alija's son, he was a policeman and he had a mask on his face.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This was a civilian police platoon called Manevar; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JOZO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: They were known as the reserve police. They were attached to the regular police.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. You said that the people that were looting were mostly unknown to you, villagers of other villages who came at night and sometimes during the day as well.

utterances.speaker: JOZO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: During the daytime. They did it openly. The police helped them to load the stuff and to take it away. There was a tractor that had broken down. And I asked, "Whose is it?" "It's that is policeman's," they said. I know exactly whose it was. That was how the police protected us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Refugees, Muslim families that had fled from other parts of Bosnia they had been expelled from, had moved into some houses; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JOZO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. It was stated that refugees should go to Susanj. It was written on a window in Zenica. There was a poster stuck on a window saying that refugees could go to Susanj because there were empty houses there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Markovic, is it true that during the conflict and after it you were not in Susanj for several days and you were not a witness of the way in which some houses were set on fire or of the way in which they were looted during that period?

utterances.speaker: JOZO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: When I came back, I saw it. But when I wasn't there, I couldn't see it. When I came back, people were stuck on the road because they were carrying away so much stuff.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. But I understand that. But during the attack and for several days after the attack you were not a witness and you don't know exactly how the houses were damaged, burnt, or looted during that period when you were not there. When you were not there, you couldn't know what was going on. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: JOZO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you ever made statements for certain individuals about which houses were damaged or looted in your village? Did you give a statement to anyone who asked you for this information?

utterances.speaker: JOZO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: No. I don't recall that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Markovic. You are now back in your house, aren't you?

utterances.speaker: JOZO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: I am.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And your relations with your neighbours are good.

utterances.speaker: JOZO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Up to a point, because quite recently I was assaulted by a neighbour and the judge said he could be sent to prison from six months to one year. And the lawyer said between one month and six months -- no, no, I'm sorry. The lawyer said between six months to two years, yet he was sentenced to one month. That is how free I am.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Markovic, for answering my questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I'm turning to the other Defence counsel. Would anybody else like to take the floor?

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. We just have one or two questions to clarify certain points with Mr. Markovic. Cross-examined by Mr. Ibrisimovic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Markovic, on behalf of Mr. Kubura's Defence, I'm going to ask you just two questions.

utterances.speaker: JOZO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Could you speak up, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On behalf of Mr. Kubura's Defence, I'm going to ask you just two questions.

utterances.speaker: JOZO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During the day today you confirmed several times that during the time the conflicts were taking place in the region of Susanj you were absent. Or, rather, you were in Zenica yourself. That's the 8th of June, 1993, the date I am referring to. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOZO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you returned to Zenica, as you told us today -- or rather, to Susanj, I'm sorry, seven days later; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JOZO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Thereabouts. I couldn't give you an exact date. Six, seven, eight days perhaps. I didn't keep count.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But can you confirm that you returned to Susanj around the 15th of June, 1993?

utterances.speaker: JOZO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Mr. Mundis, any additional questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. The Prosecution has no questions in redirect examination for the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Mr. Markovic, that completes your testimony. You have answered the questions put to you by the Prosecution and those put to you by the Defence teams. Thank you for your contribution to ascertaining the truth. I should like to ask the people in the room with you to escort you out of the room, and we should like to thank you once again for your contribution.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me turn to the Prosecution to ask them if they have another witness for us, lined up.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, there should be an additional witness standing by in Sarajevo, Mr. Ivo Vuleta.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. We're going to wait for Madam Registrar to come back into the hall and introduce the second witness.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [via videolink] I have the second witness here, Your Honour. Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Madam Registrar, since you've just told us that you have the second witness with you, would you bring him in and introduce him, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. There seems to be a problem with getting the witness into the testifying hall, so we're going to take our usual break now, although it's just a few minutes before 10.00. They need 15 minutes to put it right. But we'll reconvene at 10.30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] [Interpretation] I would just like to check on the screen to see that the witness is there. He is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can you hear what I'm saying, sir, translated into your own language?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can. Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you give me your first and last name, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ivo Vuleta.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What is your date of birth?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please approach the microphone. The interpreters cannot hear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me repeat. What is your date of birth?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: We cannot hear the witness, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We haven't heard the witness's answer. Can you hear what I'm saying, Witness?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can hear you, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I was asking you your date of birth and place of birth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In Susanj, Zenica municipality, the 12th of May, 1945.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. What is your profession or present activity?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm a pensioner.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In 1993, what was your profession or activity at the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Retired.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Have you ever testified before a tribunal or court, or is this the first time in your life that you're testifying?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I testified in Zenica three times.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. You are now going to take the solemn declaration. In order to do so, you will read out the text on the piece of paper that the lady has shown you. Would you please go ahead and read what it says.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ivo Vuleta. I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. You may be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters note that it is very difficult to follow the witness. There is a great deal of interference.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before I give the floor to the representative of the Prosecution, let me tell you about the proceedings. You are going to answer questions that the representatives of the Office of the Prosecutor are going to ask you. Having done that, having completed the examination-in-chief, the Defence counsels for the accused will also be asking you questions. The Judges, that you should be able to see on the screen in front of you, if they deem necessary, can also ask you questions at any time. Once you have heard the questions, take your time to answer them and try to give us complete and precise answers to the questions you have been asked. If you don't understand the question, then please ask the person putting it to restate the question. As you have taken the solemn declaration to speak the truth, and as you have already told us that this isn't the first time you are testifying, you though that the solemn declaration is binding and by the same token it means that you will have to tell the truth and not give false testimony. If you lie or commit perjury and give false testimony, you must be aware of the fact that sanctions can be invoked and the prison sentence term can go up to seven years or you will be reprimanded. If you give -- if you think that you might incriminate yourself in answering questions put to you, then you can refuse to answer those questions. If the witness refuses to answer, the Trial Chamber can oblige them to do so, and in that case what the witness says cannot be held against him. I wanted to inform you comprehensively of your rights before you begin your testimony in this hearing. And we're now going to have the video conference and videolink. We can see you on the screen, although you don't have us in front of you, the Judges or the two parties, the Prosecution and the Defence counsel, and that is why we have organised the videolink which enables us to see you and to hear your answers. Without further ado, I'm going to give the floor to the representative of the Prosecution, who will be asking you questions. And you're going to see him appear on your screen. Mr. Mundis, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Examined by Mr. Mundis:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Vuleta. My name is Daryl Mundis. I'm the Prosecutor or one of the Prosecutors in this case. I'm going to ask you some questions. And if you can't hear me or either don't understand the question, please inform me and I will restate the question for you. Can you please tell the Trial Chamber where you were living in June 1993.

utterances.speaker: IVO VULETA
utterances.text: Until the 8th of June, I was in my own house. After the 8th of June, that is, as of the 9th of June, I was in Zenica, staying with my brother for ten days. And then I moved to Mala Broda, and I stayed there until the 25th of August, when I was exchanged - I don't know with whom - and driven to Vitez.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Vuleta, you told us until the 8th of June you were in your own house. Where was your house up until 8 June 1993? In what town or village was your house?

utterances.speaker: IVO VULETA
utterances.text: In Susanj, Zenica municipality.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you please briefly tell the Trial Chamber what happened on the 8th of June, 1993 in Susanj.

utterances.speaker: IVO VULETA
utterances.text: I have to start from an earlier date. On the 6th of June, in the evening we were informed that we should withdraw towards the end of the village near Ovnak, because we were told that in two days the problem with Ovnak had to be resolved. And so I withdrew to the end of the village in my car, and I went to say with my father-in-law. I spent the night in the car. On the 7th, when it dawned, the attack came from the direction of Preocica on Grahovcici and the area of Strmac. This went on until about 9.00. I went back with my wife and mother to my own house. And when we arrived, the electricity had been cut off, the water supply as well. We spent the day there. Towards the evening on the 7th of June, the attack came from the direction of Grcevine [phoen], which is a hill overlooking Susanj. From the direction of Grcevine [phoen], Racinak [phoen] and Usce. And the HVO responded, returned the fire. And then things calmed down. And then in the morning, we withdrew again. I withdrew to spend the night in the same spot. In the morning, I was awakened by shooting, and I came to a spot called Balan [phoen]. And then I walked for about 300 metres to Ovnak. And there I saw with my own eyes that houses were burning in Maljine, because you can see that area well, in Krpeljici, in the direction of Guca Gora, and there were explosions and there were two or three loud explosions that reached the end of our village. Again I withdrew towards my own house, and around 10.00 - maybe a little earlier than that, 9.30 or 10.00 - I had to leave the house with my wife and mother. And not just me but many of us. And we reached a house that provided a bit of shelter. It had a good basement. And from there we moved to Stipe Markovic's house, Kazimir's son, and from there we headed towards Ovnak under fire. We were under fire. I took my car. My wife -- or rather, the wife of the late Zoran Markovic with two children, and she was sick. And I reached Jozo Kafadar's house. And I somehow managed to get out of the car. I went to the basement, and there I found some other people and the late Kazimir Markovic and his wife were also there. And then I told them, "You go on. I cannot go any further. I am an invalid. I have both my legs amputated." And Franka said that she too couldn't move any further, and the three of us stayed in the basement of Jozo Kafadar. We were looking through the window in the cellar --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Vuleta, sorry to interrupt. But let me ask a couple of follow-on questions based on what you've said so far and then I'll tell you continue. You told us a few moments ago that you were informed that you should withdraw. You told us that right at the beginning. Who told us to withdraw from your house?

utterances.speaker: IVO VULETA
utterances.text: Yes. Zoran Markovic and his brother Fabijan came to the village and he had been warned by his neighbours, Muslims, or Bosniaks, as they are now called.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You also told us that the attack came from the direction of Preocica. Do you know who -- what force or army was directing this attack?

utterances.speaker: IVO VULETA
utterances.text: I don't know that, because I wasn't there, of course. I just know that this is directly linked to the area where -- it could have been the BH army or some other unit. I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Vuleta, in June of 1993, were you a civilian or were you a soldier?

utterances.speaker: IVO VULETA
utterances.text: Of course I was a civilian, because I lost both my legs on the 14th of February.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter apologises. I missed the year.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Vuleta, could you please again tell us the year in which you lost both of your legs.

utterances.speaker: IVO VULETA
utterances.text: The 14th of February, 1988, in the ironworks in Zenica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Vuleta, when I interrupted you, you told us that you and some other people were in the basement of Jozo Kafadar. Can you please continue with the story, picking up from that basement.

utterances.speaker: IVO VULETA
utterances.text: After that, when we looked through the window, I saw that they were carrying a wounded man. I thought it was my son, you see, and I panicked. And then others explained that it wasn't my son, that it was Fabijan Laus from Cukle. However, after that, when they passed, I saw a soldier going and shooting in the direction in which the able-bodied had left the basement. Some 30 metres after him came another soldier, and then again 30 metres behind him came a third soldier who had a black beard, a cap on his head. And he turned around with his rifle and opened fire on the windows of my sister's house. Now, why he did that, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Vuleta, do you know which army or unit the soldier or soldiers that you saw shooting were with?

utterances.speaker: IVO VULETA
utterances.text: I couldn't see any insignia on them because they were about 30 metres away.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you please tell the Trial Chamber how long you remained in the basement of Jozo Kafadar.

utterances.speaker: IVO VULETA
utterances.text: Not long. Maybe half an hour, not more. And then on the pavement next to the house, one could hear steps. So I said to Kazimir and Franka, "Here's a visitor arriving." That's what I said. However, somebody I knew came through the door, Raif Rizvic. I didn't know that his real name was Ragib. And above his head a bullet flew into the wall. He bent his head. He fired a bullet. He cursed our Ustasha mothers. He chased us out of the basement, and I said, "Raif, things were not like this when we went to school together." He chased us out. He walked along the pavement. As I carry crutches, I went along the grass and we reached Jozo Kafadar's stable, when Franka fainted next to a trailer, and she asked for assistance. And the late Kazimir Markovic, knowing Raif as Raif, he said to Raif, "Bring me some water. My wife will die." He just said, "You go and get some water. You blew up -- you mined everything. Why should I get killed? You get killed." And he headed towards the door to get water. He followed him, and he said, "Give me your weapon." And Kazimir said, "I don't have any." And then this one said, "But you did have one." And Kazimir said, "I had a pistol. That was taken away from me a long time ago." And he took out his wallet to show him the certificate. They reached the smoke room of Jozo Kafadar. And then whether it was to frighten him or not, he fired three bullets. And I never learnt from the doctor how many bullets were fired into Kazimir himself. He fell to the ground, and Raif Rizvic called me -- or rather, Franka cried out, "Raif, why did you kill Kazimir?" And he said, "Keep quiet or I'll kill you too." However, he asked me, "Is this your car?" And before that, I said, "Don't make me go anywhere without a car because I don't have any legs and I need the car." And then he asked me, "Is this your car?" And I said, "Yes, it is." He said, "I wounded him. Help me carry him to the car and drive him to hospital." I asked him, "Why did you wound him?" And I apologise for saying, and he just waved his hand and said, "Fuck it." But he did help me carry him into the car. Kazimir was in the front seat and Franka behind me, and I drove towards Zenica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Vuleta -- Mr. Vuleta, I apologise for interrupting. Do you recall what Raif Rizvic was wearing at the time this event that you just described took place?

utterances.speaker: IVO VULETA
utterances.text: He didn't have a cap on his head. It was raining. His hair was all over the place. But he had a camouflage uniform on him, pants, and a vest, whatever.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Vuleta, did you in fact take Kazimir to the hospital on that day?

utterances.speaker: IVO VULETA
utterances.text: I said to him, "Raif, both parties are going to shoot at me." And he said to me, "Let your people kill you. Mine will not." And he raised his right arm, and he said, "Don't fire at this car." He pointed his finger. Now, who he was speaking to, I don't know. I didn't see them. I got to the road, and I drove off as quickly as I possibly could. I never used to drive so quickly. One bullet hit the back window next to Stanko Markovic's house, and another bullet hit the door near Tomo Vuleta's house. And then I reached the wood, and from then on I had no problems up until the bridge next to the store, where there's a school and a shop there. And when I reached the bridge, I suppose God wanted it that way, I noticed mines on the bridge. They were big mines, about 30 or 40 centimetres in diameter. So I didn't dare drive on. I honked my horn. And then a man peeped behind the corner of the shop, and I told him, "Move away the mines. I have a wounded man in the car." So they did come out and they removed the mines, and they ordered me to park in front of the shop. They asked me, "Who is wounded?" And I said that this man was wounded. "Is the woman wounded?" I said, "No." "Are you wounded?" Because I had my crutches with me. I said no. "Well, why are you carrying crutches?" I said that I was an invalid from such-and-such a date, that I had lost my legs in the ironworks. Then they ordered me and Franka to go to the prison in the school in Pojske. I said that I was driving Kazimir because he was my neighbour. He again ordered me to keep quiet and just to go to the prison.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Vuleta --

utterances.speaker: IVO VULETA
utterances.text: I didn't want to do that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Vuleta, when was the next time you returned to Susanj?

utterances.speaker: IVO VULETA
utterances.text: When we were put in prison, myself and Franka, we found Ivo Krdic [phoen], Zvonko Srtic [phoen], and Jozo Markovic all from the village of Konjevici in the prison. And we stayed there until nightfall. Then priests were brought there from Brajkovici, Frano Krizanac, Pero Karajica, two nuns whose names I don't know, and Ana Matosevic. Then women were brought there, women and children and the other men -- there was a total of nine men in the prison and the others were women and children. Then we spent the night there. At about 9.00, somebody they called the chief came. He was short, he had black hair, a well-trimmed beard. And he advised us not to go to the village because they couldn't provide security. They told us to go to the town, because it would be better there. However, we didn't listen to what he was saying. We headed towards the village. But I said to him, "Chief, as they call you, my car has been taken away from me and a wounded man was taken off. I would like my car to be returned to me, because it's my aid." And he ordered the policemen, who had insignia on them, he ordered the policemen to give me back my car. But they -- somebody they called Isak, who was some sort of a commander at the checkpoint, he promised he would give me back my car. And I waited, and a soldier brought the car. And he told him to give me the car, that I was an invalid, and that I needed it, and that the chief had ordered it. However, this soldier refused the order. He picked up a telephone device, a Motorola or whatever it was called. He took it from this Isak, and he spoke to the chief and said, "Until I finish my job, he cannot get his car." And he drove off in that car. My wife was with me. I stayed behind the other people because all the other people had left for Susanj, about 80 of them. And I stayed there with my wife. And when I saw that nothing would come of it, the guys who knew me and saw me there, Enver Spahic from Nebrovci [phoen], he suggested that he could drive me home. He knew I had no legs, and he did repairs on tractors, and we were good acquaintances. He picked me up in his car and drove me to the village, to the crossroads in the middle of the village. He was being cursed at because he had driven an Ustasha. "You too should be killed," they said. I came out of the car, and I said, "Enver, take care of yourself. Never mind me." And so I walked about 100 metres from the crossroads to my house. When I reached my house, my mother had already arrived there. The door had been broken on both floors of the house. My radio set, my video recorder had been taken away. All the things had been turned upside down. And about 50 cloths had been taken away. I wondered why -- dishcloths. I kept quiet. I didn't dare leave the house. And when I arrived, I saw a so-called moto-cultivator, a small tractor in front of Mario Vuleta's house loading TVs, video recorders, radios, washing machines, household appliances. The same happened in front of Mario Vuleta's house. I didn't dare stay there any longer nor look around much, but I did see this. And then I reached my house, and I didn't dare come out again. However, about an hour or something later, Andja Markovic arrived. She is deceased now. Branko Vuleta, Stipo Vuleta, Ana Vuleta, Pavo Markovic's wife whose name I cannot recall, and Ivo Markovic Marinko's wife, and they said Drago Markovic -- and his real name was Dragutin, but we called him Drago -- was killed in his own house, and nothing is known about Ilija Vidosevic, Ante Vidosevic, Niko Vidosevic, Vlado Markovic, Dragun Vidosevic. Kazimir was in hospital -- left in hospital. We didn't know how he was. And then they said, "We have to go to Zenica. We mustn't stay here any longer." And 47 of us started off, and again we reached the checkpoint at Pojske, when Isak let me pass, knowing that he hadn't given me my car, and my wife. I begged him to let my mother pass as well. And he let us pass.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Vuleta --

utterances.speaker: IVO VULETA
utterances.text: But I waited for three or four hours --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Again, I apologise for interrupting, but I have a few follow-on questions to what you've told us. Do you recall the approximate time and the date that you arrived back in the village of Susanj when you witnessed all of these things that you've just told us about?

utterances.speaker: IVO VULETA
utterances.text: It was the 9th of June, at about 10.00, half past 10.00. That's when I got to my house, when we were released from prison that morning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And which year was that, sir?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you first arrived in the village on that morning, did you see any people moving about in the village?

utterances.speaker: IVO VULETA
utterances.text: There were people in uniform, and they had police insignia on their sleeves, white armbands, and it said "Police, BiH army."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What kind of uniforms were these people wearing?

utterances.speaker: IVO VULETA
utterances.text: Camouflage uniforms.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what were these people doing that you saw wearing these camouflage uniforms with police insignia?

utterances.speaker: IVO VULETA
utterances.text: At the crossroads in the middle of the village, they were standing there. They were standing there, and I said they threatened Enver, who brought me, Enver Spahic, and said that they would kill him for having driven me. I don't know what happened to Enver after that, because I went to my own house. And these others in camouflage uniform, who I said were loading up all the goods onto the tractor that I've already described.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Approximately how many homes or houses were in the village of Susanj in 1993?

utterances.speaker: IVO VULETA
utterances.text: In 1993, I think about 118 houses. That's the number. And those who made lists, they said 120 families or households, because some houses would house two families, for instance.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Vuleta, at the time you left the village on the 9th of June, 1993, the -- where was the tractor that you've told us about at that time, when you left?

utterances.speaker: IVO VULETA
utterances.text: I went from my house towards the -- towards Pojske, the village. And there's a middle bend there. The tractor stayed behind in front of Marijan Vuleta's house and I could see it in front of Marijan Vuleta's house. Whether that one was taken away or not, I don't know because I couldn't see that. There was a bend in the road, and I didn't dare look around too much either.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Vuleta, at the time you arrived in the village of Susanj in the morning of the 9th of June, 1993, what was the condition of the houses in the village?

utterances.speaker: IVO VULETA
utterances.text: Tomo Markovic's house had been set fire to by a shell on the 8th, when the attacks took place. And just the door was damaged in the other houses. All the doors were open. Otherwise, the others were left standing. They weren't burnt that day. The roofs were still on the houses. So they weren't burnt that day or the next day either.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When after the 9th of June, 1993 did you next return to the village of Susanj?

utterances.speaker: IVO VULETA
utterances.text: I don't know the date, but it was the Sunday before Easter. Because in 1995, when I arrived in Susanj for the first time afterwards, at Ovnak, where the cemetery is, we went to visit our dead. And it was the Sunday before Easter. I don't know the exact date. But anyway, it was in 1995.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Vuleta.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: The Prosecution has no further questions, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Mundis. Let me turn towards the Defence. The Defence has the floor.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Cross-examined by Ms. Residovic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Vuleta. My name is Edina Residovic. I am the Defence counsel for General Hadzihasanovic. I'm going to ask you just a few questions, and I should like to ask you to answer, please. You lost your legs in an accident at the ironworks while you were working there; is that right? On the job.

utterances.speaker: IVO VULETA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At the time, you were living and working with members of all the ethnic groups living in Zenica at the time, Serbs, Muslims, and Croats alike; is that right?

utterances.speaker: IVO VULETA
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So all these people, all your fellow workers, the people you worked with, helped you a great deal in surviving such a difficult accident and in becoming capacitated to carry on with your life and to carry on with your work, and they bought you to vehicle that you described to us; is that right?

utterances.speaker: IVO VULETA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In answer to a question from my learned colleague, you said that two days before the fighting took place on the 8th of June that Fabijan and Zoran Markovic warned you and told you to leave the village, or rather, to go towards Ovnak; is that right?

utterances.speaker: IVO VULETA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: To the best of your knowledge, Fabijan and Zoran Markovic at the time were members of the Croatian Defence Council; is that right?

utterances.speaker: IVO VULETA
utterances.text: I suppose so. I don't really know. I suppose so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Otherwise, all military-able men from your village belonged to the Frankopan Brigade and their company had its headquarters at Grahovcici; is that right?

utterances.speaker: IVO VULETA
utterances.text: I don't know that. I don't know who they belonged to or what they belonged to, but I do know that the HVO as such did exist.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: IVO VULETA
utterances.text: However, which brigade they belonged to, I can't say.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. The next thing I want to ask you is this: The wounded man Kazimir Markovic, at the request of Ragib Rizvic you took him to hospital in Zenica; is that right?

utterances.speaker: IVO VULETA
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In Pojske, you were stopped by the army, by soldiers, and you yourself were taken to the school building and the soldiers took the wounded Kazimir to hospital in Zenica themselves; is that right?

utterances.speaker: IVO VULETA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In response to a question from the Trial Chamber, you said that you testified several times before the court in Zenica.

utterances.speaker: IVO VULETA
utterances.text: Three times.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It was a court case against Ragib Rizvic for what he had done to Kazimir; is that right?

utterances.speaker: IVO VULETA
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And Rizvic by the cantonal court in Zenica was found guilty for this act; is that right?

utterances.speaker: IVO VULETA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Vuleta. I have no further questions for you.

utterances.speaker: IVO VULETA
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. What about the other Defence team?

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. We have no questions for this witness, on behalf of Mr. Kubura. I'm grateful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Mundis, additional questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Just one or two, Mr. President, arising from the cross-examination. Re-examined by Mr. Mundis:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Vuleta, do you recall the approximate date or time period in which you testified in the court in Zenica, in the case involving Mr. Rizvic?

utterances.speaker: IVO VULETA
utterances.text: I don't know the exact date, but it was, roughly speaking, sometime in the spring or summer. It was warm weather. Before that, I gave a statement, but I can't remember --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you --

utterances.speaker: IVO VULETA
utterances.text: Anyway, Rizvic -- I don't know the date. I don't remember the date.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall which year?

utterances.speaker: IVO VULETA
utterances.text: Last year, 2003.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Vuleta.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: The Prosecution has no further questions, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Vuleta, your testimony has been completed. You answered questions put to you by the Prosecution and the Defence counsel. We should like to thank you for having contributed to establishing the truth through your testimony, and I'm now going to ask Madam Registrar to escort you out of the room you're in.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This brings us to the end of the testimonies of the two witnesses that were scheduled for today. As we still have some time left, let me ask the parties present whether they have, as Mr. Bourgon says, any representations to make or motions to raise. If there are none, if there are no problems -- but yes, Maitre Bourgon has the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Just quickly, I should like to indicate to the Trial Chamber that pursuant to a ruling by the Chamber we filed a motion with more specific information with respect to evidence admitted in other cases. And we, however, sent out the wrong information file. So during the weekend, we sent in a new file which was edited with the right text. So, Mr. President, I hope that on Monday morning we'll be able to distribute this second, corrected text. I was told by the registrar that both texts were distributed. But I'd like to draw the attention of the Trial Chamber that the meritorious text is the second text. So just take into account the second text, which will be translated in English for the Prosecution in due course. And it regards resources of the Registry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What is the date of the second text, Maitre Bourgon? Because I have seen the two texts myself. The second is what date?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The second, Mr. President, we put the same date on it, but it was sent out to the Registry on Sunday, the 14th.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I seem to remember that above the text it said the hour, it stated the hour as well. So we can check that out. We'll check out which is the right text, because I think that they had the time, the departure time, the time that your fax was sent out.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. Both texts had two different numbers, but both were registered. So I hope that on Monday morning we'll be able to replace the first document with the second document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I'm looking to the Prosecution for any additional remarks. Does the Prosecution intend to respond? Once -- in view of the fact that the document has several pages with additional points of law set out in it, because it is the jurisprudence from a military tribunal following General Rendulic's prosecution, and the subject is developed in this document, would the Prosecution like to respond? And within what time frame?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, the Prosecution would certainly like to respond. And if memory serves me correctly, the Chamber had ordered the Prosecution to respond by Friday, the 19th of -- Friday, the 19th of March, that being this Friday. As of this morning, neither Mr. Withopf nor myself have seen the revised version or perhaps -- let me correct that. We have only to date received one version of the Defence motion. I'm not sure if that's the corrected one or if that was the previously filed one. Perhaps, because the Registry either hand-paginates or electronically paginates them, if I could get the Registry page numbers of the final and corrected version, then I can ascertain if in fact we have the correct motion. And I can get that from the registrar immediately after today's proceedings, unless he has it handy. We -- we certainly -- my case manager says she's just received it, so I think we do have that. We certainly will be responding. At this point, Mr. President, it might be premature for me to give you an assurance that we will in fact meet the Friday deadline for filing. However, if it does appear that we might need some additional time, I will certainly make an application to Your Honours for an additional period of time in order to complete that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] An oral request will be quite sufficient. I noted the last time that on the 8th of April we will have a hearing for the admission of documents that are not contested by the Defence and which will be tendered by the Prosecution. I should also like to make it quite clear in this connection - but of course we will wait for the response of the Defence in relation to the famous consolidated list - however, regarding the documents that are not contested by the Defence, it would be desirable once you have been informed of the position of the Defence to put these documents into one binder and to plan several binders which will be distributed to everyone. And, of course, a binder for the Registry. And then these exhibits put -- following the order from your consolidated list would allow everyone to find their way around simply. That is the method that I would suggest, which would ensure efficiency of work for us, that is, as far as the documents are concerned. The same will apply for the famous 858 documents. If the Defence decides to tender them at some point in time, then too this method of putting them in binders would facilitate things. On the other hand, the exhibits that are contested, the documents that are contested and that will be tendered during testimony of witnesses, will be admitted one by one as has been indicated, opening the possibility - and I turn to Mr. Withopf for this - that the documents contested by the Defence during General Reinhardt's testimony, then those documents that you intend to tender could also be collected in a single binder, which would be useful for handling purposes during the testimony. And then you will indicate that you intend to tender such and such a number of a document, the Defence will contest it, and the Chamber will weigh the thing out and decide.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, we will certainly follow the suggestions just made by you, Mr. President. There's one issue, however, I wish to address: It's our understanding that on the 8th of April the documents will be given an exhibit number. It appears to be advisable, in order to facilitate the work of the registry and both parties, to give such exhibits which are not contested by the Defence exhibit numbers earlier on. That would allow the Prosecution to order their -- to put together their documents in a numerical order following the exhibit number given by the registry. So if at an earlier point in time such documents could be given an exhibit number, that would be beneficial for all parties involved.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Quite. Once we have the position of the Defence regarding the mentioned documents, then if, shall we say, there are 30 or 40 that are not contested, we will know that there will be at least 30 numbers following a certain order. Then we can preempt before the 8th of April the numbers, because those documents will have been officially admitted on the 8th of April. However, the registry will tell us which the numbers are, which would respond to your suggestion. On the other hand, of course, the contested documents will not have any numbers. And we can only mark them for identification or after the testimony, if they are admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The registrar, in order to carry out his task, tells me that the contested documents could be marked for identification, but we'll reflect upon that possibility. However, we will see. Because clearly, in view of the number of documents, if we preempt numbers and mark for identification, that will mean that the documents that come after that should follow the logical order. And if we do not admit those that have been marked for identification, then we will have numbers missing in the order. But in any event, we will decide in due course. Are there any other questions or matters to be raised regarding the plan for tomorrow? We have witnesses planned. And I give the floor to Mr. Withopf to tell us about the two planned witnesses for tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, as it stands now, both witnesses will be made available tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I've also noted that on your memorandum for the next week three persons have been envisaged between Monday, the 22nd of March, Tuesday, Wednesday, Thursday, and Friday. There are three persons for the whole week. But as their testimony risks to be quite long, that is probably why that has been planned in this way. As you know, because of the ceremony tomorrow morning, we cannot have the hearing in the morning, unfortunately, which will force everyone to come tomorrow at 2.15. So we'll have our hearing tomorrow at 2.15 continuing the proceedings of today. And after that, we will go back to morning sessions for Thursday and Friday, as usual. Having said everything, I thank everyone, and I invite you to be back here tomorrow at 2.15.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 17th of March, 2004, at 2.15 p.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 11.31 a.m.,
